judged.justification: Frames Dionysius as Proclean in a discussion of the Oration's own mystical sources.
Reverses the received individualist reading of the Oration.

rel.basis: The editors report the etymology Methathronius, he who is next to the throne of God, which bears out Copenhaver's description of Metatron as stationed behind the throne of the Almighty.

quotes.t: The Oration has said nothing yet about Kabbalah when the orator announces that “with their more secret theology, Hebrews too sometimes
transform the blessed Enoch into an angel of divinity, whom they call מטטרון”—Metatron.
But the Oration, supplying none of this context, introduces the angel and a “more secret theology” with hints about Kabbalah entirely beyond the grasp of Christians.

judged.justification: Explains the Metatron reference as a deliberately concealed Kabbalistic signal.

rel.basis: Copenhaver prints T2K10 with Metatron as the Kabbalists' name for what Orpheus calls Pallas and the rest, which presupposes Wirszubski's proposal that the blank in the editio princeps is to be filled with the Hebrew name of Metatron.

Both give T2K10 as saying that what the Kabbalists call Metatron is what Orpheus calls Pallas, Zoroaster the paternal mind, Hermes the son of God, Pythagoras wisdom and Parmenides the intelligible sphere.
Both say Pico's Kabbalistic thesis amalgamates Metatron with Orpheus' Pallas, Zoroaster's paternal mind, Hermes' son of God, Pythagoras' wisdom and Parmenides' intelligible sphere.

judged.justification: States the Metatron-Pallas equation of 2K10 in Copenhaver's translation.

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes Abulafia in a text translated for Pico.

rel.basis: Both say Metatron is identified with the Active or Agent Intellect, notably by Abulafia, in texts that reached Pico.

Both quote a Latin text translated for Pico in which the intellect that brings ours from potency to act, separate from all matter, is called Mattatron, prince of the face or faces, and the philosophers' agent intellect.

Howlett quotes Abulafia calling the Metatron the intellect that actualizes ours from potency, detached from matter, prince of the world and angel of the Face, called by philosophers the Agent Intellect; Copenhaver quotes the same doctrine in a text translated for Pico.

judged.justification: Reads the angelic life as a soteriological aspiration for fallen humans.

rel.basis: Edelheit's reading of the Oration's Cherubic purification and Copenhaver's account both hold that humans in the flesh are called first to the Cherubic life, following the Dionysian purify-illuminate-perfect scheme.

judged.justification: Ties the three orders to the Dionysian triad and to the Zohar's angelic leaders.

rel.basis: Edelheit reports that Thomas, in Quodlibet 5 q.4, 'following Pseudo-Dionysius closely, stresses the hierarchy between hierarchies and orders of angels and even among angels in the same order'; this corroborates Copenhaver's claim that 'Dionysius the Areopagite was the first to organize nine ranks of angels into three orders of three', since Thomas's later refinement presupposes exactly that Dionysian ordering.

judged.justification: Establishes the Dionysian, not Hebrew, provenance of the Thrones.

rel.basis: Still and Copenhaver agree that Pico arranged the highest three orders so that Thrones govern the active life, Cherubs the contemplative middle, and Seraphs the unitive love at the summit.

judged.justification: States the tripartite scheme (agency, psychology, substance) in one place.
Shows Pico's Thrones-as-judgment departs from Dionysius and follows Psalm and Gregory.

quotes.t: The Areopagite’s nine ranks became canonical for Christians, though Jewish tradition often preferred ten groups. In a Kabbalist text known to Pico, the names were those that he used in the Conclusions, while changing the order:
There are nine hierarchies of angels, whose names are Cherubim, Seraphim, Hasmalim, Haiot, Aralim, Tarsisim, Ophanim, Thephsarim, and Isim.

rel.basis: Both say the nine angelic hierarchies of thesis 1K2 (Cherubim, Seraphim, Hasmalim, Haiot, Aralim, Tarsisim, Ophanim, Thephsarim, Isim) come from a Kabbalistic text known to Pico that gives the same names in a different order.

Copenhaver says Jewish tradition often preferred ten groups while the Kabbalist text known to Pico lists nine, which bears out Wirszubski's point that nine is unusual against the usual ten in Jewish sources.

judged.justification: Keeps the Hebrew nine hierarchies distinct from Dionysius' nine.

quotes.t: T1K30 No angel with six wings ever changes. The immutable angels were Seraphim and Cherubim, but Pico mentioned Cherubim first, ready for humans to emulate in a “Cherubic life,” whereas Seraphs blazed beyond reach and Thrones reached down toward “lower …

judged.justification: Equates the Kabbalistic Hasmalim with the Dionysian Thrones.

rel.basis: Still and Copenhaver agree that Pico's Dionysian ordering has judgment (Thrones) and love (Seraphim) needing the Cherub's illuminating knowledge between them.

judged.justification: Gives Copenhaver's summary of the ascent in the order judging, knowing, loving.

quotes.t: The Cherub is the “knot” that ties these “primary minds” together, said Pico. Pallas, goddess of wisdom and “protector of contemplative philosophy,” governs this angelic order. Since thesis T2K10 identifies “what Orpheus names Pallas” as Metatron—within the Seraphic fire surrounding …

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers the Pallas-Metatron-Wisdom identification from thesis T2K10 and the location of Metatron within the Seraphic fire.

open.t: Copenhaver locates Metatron within the Seraphic fire yet has Pallas govern the Cherubic order; the passage does not explain how the two placements fit.

rel.basis: The editors say the order of Pallas is that of cherubic contemplation between the seraphim (love) and thrones (justice); Copenhaver says Pallas governs the Cherubic order, the knot that ties the primary minds.

judged.justification: Reads the Order of Pallas passage as Kabbalistic: the Cherub governed by Pallas is Metatron and S2.

quotes.t: Pico, who could see Pallas in this Kabbalist way, also learned mysteries from Proclus, from other pagan Platonists and from Ficino, their master explicator.
Although Pallas actually had no role in the Chaldean theology, Proclus replaced her with Hecate, also well-armed and philosophy’s protector in the Oracles.

bears.note: Ficino, as master explicator of pagan Platonists, is a channel for Pico's Pallas material.
Ficino mediates Proclus to Pico; Copenhaver calls him Pico's friend.

rel.basis: Copenhaver states that 'much of the ancient theology' Ficino found in Plato's dialogues 'had already been explicated by Proclus, whose insights Ficino used in his own commentaries', so that Pico 'had abundant help from Ficino'; Allen independently proposes that Pico met the Neoplatonists' reading of the later dialogues 'in the voluminous scholarly commentaries of Marsilio Ficino' -- both identify Ficino's commentaries as Pico's channel to this Neoplatonic material.

warrants.t: An inference from Ficino's letter to Lorenzo about Pico's arrival and the later ten-year gap.

bears.note: Copenhaver characterizes Pico as arrogant and careless even with friends, and infers earlier friction with Ficino.

judged.justification: Adds a hint of friction beneath Ficino's celebratory account of the meeting.

bears.note: Contrasts Ficino's explicatory practice with Pico's deliberate mystification.

judged.justification: Sets Ficino's method against Pico's for the same Platonic material.
Makes the Cherubic life, not the Seraphic, the practical model.
Ties the Kabbalistic thesis to Dionysian apophatic theology.

quotes.t: At the top of the angelic hierarchy, as described by Dionysius, were Thrones to cleanse sinners, Cherubs to enlighten them, and Seraphs to perfect them.

judged.justification: Places the Cherubic light below the final mystical dissolution.
Presents Dionysius as a theurgic Neoplatonist in the setting of the Oration.

quotes.t: More useful to Pico, perhaps, was a Book of Imaginary Circles by Ibn al-Sid al-Batalyawsi, known to Jews in the prince’s Italy. Convinced that higher realities transcend ordinary geometry, Batalyawsi envisioned a straight line or ladder running between two circles …

open.t: Whether Pico used Batalyawsi is left open by the word 'perhaps'.

judged.justification: Reads the Job passage as Kabbalistic angelology (Michael and Gabriel) not only ethics.
Links the two archangels to sefirotic positions.

rel.basis: Copenhaver reads the Oration's angel magic as a theurgy that emulates Enoch's transformation into Metatron, which bears out Howlett's claim that Enoch as Metatron is the model of the seeker's transformation into an angel.

judged.justification: Ties the Job peace to angel magic and Metatron.
Names the three sources of the Oration's mysticism in one sentence.

open.t: The quotation about the mid-day light is cited to a source in Copenhaver's note 43 (not read here); it is not clear from the passage alone whether the words are Augustine's or Pico's paraphrase.

rel.basis: Copenhaver reports that Augustine's interpretation of the Psalmist's morning-noon-evening prayer supplies the source Still reads as showing that the highest illumination needs an infusion from beyond the soul.

judged.justification: Maps the three archangels onto the curriculum and the Sefirot.

quotes.t: The very first of Pico’s Kabbalist theses (T1K1) introduces Michael, stationed below these loftier spirits but a high priest nonetheless. The purpose of his priesthood is for saints to be sacrificed by a good death of the kiss.

Souls to be saved must rise through the place where Abraham presides and where Michael “sacrifices the souls of the just.” In theosophical space, the place is S4, just beneath the supreme triad where annihilation in the Godhead waits.

judged.justification: Places Michael's priesthood at S4.
Presents Michael as a benign messenger of death and the giver of the priesthood of theology.

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers what Ficino and Poliziano knew; no direct evidence is quoted at this point.

bears.note: Copenhaver has Ficino know only 'more or less' what Pico was doing.
Copenhaver has Poliziano know only 'more or less' what Pico was doing.
Flavius and other Jews helped Pico with Kabbalah and understood his project best.

copenhaver2019-angels:049.hedge_words: will have known what their friend was up to, more or less

judged.justification: Assigns Flavius, not Ficino, the best understanding of the Kabbalistic project.

open.t: Whether Pico deliberately concealed angel-magic while advertising natural magic is posed as a question, answered only that the magic theses 'suggest so'.

judged.justification: Proposes that the Oration's natural magic conceals an angel-magic visible only in the Kabbalistic theses.

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes Abulafia on the Agent Intellect and its names.

rel.basis: Copenhaver quotes Abulafia giving Cherub, Enoch and Metatron as names of the Agent Intellect, and Wirszubski says Abulafia identifies Metatron with the Active Intellect.

Wirszubski's Latin preface has the archangel set over the hierarchy of angels called intellectus agens or Mattatron; Copenhaver's Abulafia quotation says the Agent Intellect, called Metatron, rules over the hierarchy of angels.

Howlett says the Active Intellect is expressed as Hokmah but also as Enoch, Metatron and the Cherubic realm, and her notes cite Copenhaver (2019), whose text quotes Abulafia giving Cherub, Enoch and Metatron as names of the Agent Intellect.

judged.justification: Links the Cherub, Enoch and Metatron with the Agent Intellect.

bears.note: Copenhaver contrasts Pico's route to supernatural magic through Kabbalah with Ficino's use of occult qualities.

rel.basis: Copenhaver notes that Pico, unlike Ficino, did not turn to 'the occult qualities of scholastic metaphysics' but used Kabbalah to reach supernatural magic; this supports Howlett's broader claim that 'Kabbalism did not have such a distinctive role in Ficino', both identifying Kabbalah as specifically Pico's own addition beyond Ficino's approach.

judged.justification: States what the Oration does not say about angels in its defence of magic.

quotes.t: He wanted them to “turn into separate angels” by attaining the state of prophecy and to be “saved by this from natural death on the day of their . . . death and live forever.”
including rites to join with Metatron, the angel prince identified by Abulafia with the Agent Intellect.

Mystical union with the Intellect or Metatron eradicates the self. In Abulafia’s conception, however, the self vanishes not only within the Mind but also in favor of others because the mystic’s role is messianic as well as prophetic.

rel.basis: Both say that Abulafia identified the angel Metatron with the Agent (Active) Intellect.
Howlett says the mystic literally becomes the Agent Intellect, the human self dissolving; Copenhaver says mystical union with the Intellect or Metatron eradicates the self.

judged.justification: Connects Abulafian union with the Intellect to the Oration's angelic transformation.

open.t: Whether Pico actually learned that Metatron is the Messiah, El Shaddai and the Shekinah is posed only as a condition.

rel.basis: Howlett's Abulafia quotation says the intellect's name is Sadday, like its master's, and its cognomen is Metatron; this is text for Copenhaver's claim that Metatron was addressed as Shaddai and Shekinah.

judged.justification: Connects Metatron with the Christian Trinity via Shaddai and the Shekinah.

bears.note: The passage explains why Pico's angel-magic could be seen as dangerous for a Christian.

rel.basis: The editors say Pico identifies Michael with the sefirah Keter, the symbol of the priesthood; Copenhaver places Michael's Love at S4 in sefirotic space, so the two assign Michael to different sefirot.

open.t: What the Oration means by a finished metaphysics of angelic forms is left open by Copenhaver.

rel.basis: Copenhaver lists the orders of angels and the fall of the demons among the doctrines Pico says the Kabbalistic books confirm, the same list as in Pico's Oration text.

judged.justification: Grounds Pico's derivation of the Trinity in Proclean triads.

bears.note: Pico asked to borrow Ficino's copy of Iamblichus.

judged.justification: Places Pico's angel theses in the ordinary scholastic curriculum rather than magic.

open.t: Whether Pico knew Abu Ma'shar's identification of Idris with Enoch and Hermes is left open.

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers a possible link between Flavius's history with Cibò and the pope's view of Pico.

bears.note: Copenhaver offers Flavius's earlier friction with Cibò as a possible factor in Innocent VIII's judgment of Pico.
Flavius had alienated Cibò before Cibò was pope.
Background to the condemnation of thirteen theses.

judged.justification: Offers a personal rather than doctrinal factor in the condemnation.

bears.note: On this reading the Oration's angelic message was undetectable by the intended Christian audience.

judged.justification: Puts the change into angels, by magic and Kabbalah, at the centre of the Oration.

rel.basis: Copenhaver has the Oration exhort humans to become angels and then to be annihilated in God, becoming absolutely one with him; Howlett says that if the Active Intellect is the end point, it is not unio mystica with the hidden God or even Keter but a form of noesis, so the goal is narrower than union with God.

judged.justification: Reads the Oration as an exhortation to angel magic.
Reverses the reading of dignitas as human dignity: it is an angelic rank.
Characterizes the Cherubic life as bodiless and sexless.
States what the Oration does and does not show of Kabbalah.

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes the Asclepius on animating idols with the souls of demons or angels.

judged.justification: Explains Pico's silence about Hermetic angel-and-demon idol magic.
Frames the Sefirot as actors, not angels.

rel.basis: Both give Pico's statement that a man who cultivates his intellectual seeds will be an angel and a son of God.

judged.justification: Angels are fixed in nature while humans can become angels.

rel.basis: Both give Pico's Oration sentence that the more secret Hebrew theology transforms Enoch into an angel of divinity, named in Hebrew Metatron; Copenhaver's version adds the Latin gloss that spiritual intelligence makes an angel.
Both give Pico's statement that spiritual intelligence, not separation from the body, is what makes an angel.

judged.justification: The Oration's only mention of Metatron by name comes in a list of metamorphoses.

rel.basis: Both give Pico's exhortation to fly to the court where seraphim, cherubim and thrones hold first place and to rival their dignity and glory.
Both give Pico's characterisation of the three ranks: the seraph burns with love, the cherub shines with intelligence, the throne stands firm in judgment.

judged.justification: The three orders correspond to love, intelligence, judgment.

rel.basis: Still has contemplation of the cherubim between the thrones' active life and the seraphim's unitive love; Copenhaver translates the Oration passage in which the Cherub prepares us for Seraphic fire and lights our way toward the judgment of Thrones.
Both give Pico's statement that the cherub, in the middle, prepares us by its light for the seraphic fire and lights our way to the judgment of the thrones.

judged.justification: The ordering judging-knowing-loving is not the Dionysian order.
The Order of Pallas is named here, not glossed; the gloss is in T2K10.

rel.basis: Black's paraphrase and Copenhaver's translation both give Pico's Pauline vision of the cherubic hosts as cleansed, then illuminated, then perfected.
Both give Pico's account of Jacob's ladder, the contemplative angels moving up and down it in turns.
Both give Pico's statement that the peace God makes on high is announced by descending angels so that men, ascending, are made into angels.
Still and Copenhaver both read the midday light passage as inflaming the Seraphim and, at the same time, illuminating the Cherubim.

judged.justification: The Oration says only that Kabbalah teaches 'the orders of angels' in agreement with Dionysius.

rel.basis: Borghesi directs readers to Conclusiones 1.19.2, according to Themistius, for the Enoch-Metatron transfiguration; Copenhaver's translation of the Themistius thesis states that the Agent Intellect that only illuminates is in Themistius what Metatron is in Kabbalah.
Howlett cites Conclusion 28>2 for Pico making the angelic hierarchy ten; Copenhaver's translation of that thesis (1K2) states that there are nine hierarchies of angels and lists nine names.

judged.justification: States the nine Hebrew hierarchies in Pico's own thesis, kept distinct from Dionysian nine.

rel.basis: Borghesi directs readers to Conclusiones 2.11.10 for the Enoch-Metatron transfiguration; Copenhaver's translation of 2K10 gives the text of that thesis, in which Metatron is identified with what the ancient theologians named Pallas and the rest.

judged.justification: Pico's own wording of the Metatron-Pallas equation.
Places angel and rational soul on a scale beneath a God who is not an intellect.

quotes.t: In T2K10, a space to be filled by a Hebrew word is blank in the printed edition of the Conclusions; Ebgi 2014, 215–225, prefers Hokmah, S2, following a commentary by Francesco Zorzi; Wirszubski’s choice of Metatron seems better, however, because …

warrants.t: Copenhaver argues from the match with the other entities named in the thesis and from another thesis that identifies the Agent Intellect with Metatron.

open.t: Which Hebrew word stood in the blank of T2K10 (Metatron or Hokmah) is disputed; Ebgi and Wirszubski differ.

rel.basis: Copenhaver, weighing the blank in T2K10, says Wirszubski's choice of Metatron is the better one because the Agent Intellect is explicitly identified with Metatron by another thesis and matches the other names listed; this is a further argument for Wirszubski's proposal that the blank stood for Metatron.

judged.justification: Records that the Metatron reading of 2K10 is an editorial restoration, not a printed word.

rel.basis: Howlett says Metatron can also be the ascended Enoch, the apotheosis of the seeker and a model of the mystic's transformation; Copenhaver's glossary calls Metatron a model for mystical union because he was once a human, Enoch.

open.t: The glossary calls the knot of primary minds 'the highest angels' whereas the chapter has the Cherub tie the knot; the two are not reconciled in the glossary.

rel.basis: The editors say the Orphean Pallas is associated with the cabalists' Metatron in Conclusiones 2.11.10, and Copenhaver's glossary says that at T2K10 Pallas is Metatron; both take Pallas as a name for Metatron in the thesis.

judged.justification: Glossary summary of the Pallas-Metatron identification.

rel.basis: Allen identifies the Pseudo-Areopagite as 'Proclus' great sixth century disciple'; Copenhaver's glossary independently describes him as a 'Christian contemporary of Proclus' who 'wrote around 500 CE in a Neoplatonist way' -- the same identification of Dionysius as Proclus's Neoplatonist disciple/contemporary rather than Paul's convert.

judged.justification: Dates the angel-and-demon hierarchy of Platonism after Plotinus.
